title: Work as a project team member

lessons.title: Projects, roles and the project plan
lessons.html:
What makes work a project?

A project is a temporary piece of work with a clear goal, a start and end date, a budget and a defined result. It differs from routine operations, which repeat every day. In a packhouse or grain silo, examples include installing a new sizing line before the season, upgrading a cold room, introducing a new traceability system, or preparing for a GLOBALG.A.P. or customer audit.

Typical project roles

RoleResponsibility
SponsorSenior person who approves the project and budget
Project manager / leaderPlans, coordinates and reports on progress
Team membersCarry out assigned tasks and report on them
StakeholdersAnyone affected: workers, customers, suppliers, contractors

The project plan

As a team member you must understand the plan, because your tasks fit into it. A plan usually contains:

  • Scope: what is included and, just as important, what is not.
  • Deliverables: the concrete outputs, for example a commissioned machine and trained operators.
  • Work breakdown: the work split into tasks with owners.
  • Schedule: task durations and dependencies, often shown as a Gantt chart. Some tasks cannot start until others finish; these form the critical path, and any delay on it delays the whole project.
  • Budget and resources: money, people, equipment.
  • Risks: what could go wrong and the planned response.
  • Quality and safety requirements.

Understanding your assignment

When you receive a task, clarify: What exactly must be delivered? By when? To what standard? What resources do I have? Who do I report to? Write this down. If the deadline or resources are unrealistic, say so early with reasons, rather than failing quietly later.

lessons.title: Contributing effectively to the team
lessons.html:
Doing your part

Projects succeed when each member delivers reliably and communicates openly. Your contribution is measured on results, but also on how well you help the team work together.

Managing your tasks

  1. Break your task into steps and estimate the time for each.
  2. Schedule your work around operational duties; agree priorities with your line supervisor and project leader.
  3. Track progress against the plan. Keep simple notes of what was done and what is outstanding.
  4. Report progress at agreed intervals, using facts: percentage complete, issues, help needed.
  5. Escalate problems early: a late supplier delivery, a safety concern, a cost overrun. Early warning gives the team options.

Team dynamics

Teams usually go through stages: forming (getting to know each other), storming (disagreements about roles and approach), norming (agreeing how to work) and performing (working well together). Conflict is normal in the storming stage. Handle it by focusing on the problem, not the person, listening to understand, and agreeing on facts before solutions.

Good team behaviour

  • Keep commitments; if you cannot, tell the team as soon as you know.
  • Share information and knowledge freely.
  • Respect diversity of language, culture, gender and experience.
  • Support colleagues who are struggling.
  • Take part in meetings: prepare, stay on topic, and follow up on action items assigned to you.

Change control

Requests to add work or change specifications must go through the project leader, because changes affect time, cost and risk. Do not quietly expand the scope of your task.

Closing the project

At the end, deliverables are handed over and signed off, documents are filed, and the team reviews lessons learned: what went well, what to improve. Give honest input; it improves the next project.

Key points

  • A project is temporary, with a goal, schedule, budget and defined result.
  • Understand scope, deliverables, schedule and your role in the plan.
  • Clarify each assignment and raise unrealistic expectations early.
  • Report progress with facts and escalate problems early.
  • Changes go through the project leader; capture lessons learned at the end.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a project from routine operations?

options.text: It is temporary with a defined goal, start and end
The safest walking route in the packhouse
The chain of dependent tasks where any delay delays the whole project

quiz.question: You realise your task will finish a week late because a supplier is delayed. What should you do?

options.text: Tell the project leader early and explain the issue
Say nothing and hope to catch up
Change the deadline in the plan yourself
Hand the task to someone else without telling anyone

quiz.question: A colleague asks you to add an extra feature to the new line that is not in the plan. What is the correct response?

options.text: Add it and charge it to another budget
Refer the request to the project leader as a change request
